info.title: Hanzo Cloud API
info.description: Package integrations is how your org connects third-party accounts like Slack, and revokes them.

get.summary: Lists the caller's OWN connectors across every provider — the set `hanzo connector ls` prints.
get.description:
Lists the caller's OWN connectors across every provider — the set
`hanzo connector ls` prints. Rows are keyed (org,user), so this can never
surface another user's connector, and no secret is in the view.

get.summary: Lists the USER-plane provider cards.
get.description:
Lists the USER-plane provider cards. It is not the org
catalog at /v1/provider and the two are not a duplicate of one another: a
provider declares its custody plane, and the planes are disjoint, so a
user-scoped provider 404s on the org surface and vice versa. Hence the
catalog of what a
user can connect, and how. Modes derive from capabilities (Device/Adopt/Verify
— Mount asserts at least one), never from a parallel kind enum.

delete.summary: Forgets a connector: every custodied secret, then the row.
delete.description:
Forgets a connector: every custodied secret, then the row.
Idempotent — dropping a never-connected id still answers {disconnected:true}
(disconnect() parity). No provider Revoke: none of the user-plane providers
exposes a revoke endpoint.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
ID is the connector id, provider + ":" + label ("openai:default") — the
auth-profile-id shape. Another user's id is simply no row, so 404.

post.description:
Forces a token rotation for a connected connector, ahead of the
automatic rotation a token read would do inside the expiry window. Only

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:

get.summary: Hands the custodied access token to its owner — the ONE place custody exits.
get.description:
Hands the custodied access token to its owner — the ONE place
custody exits. The (org,user)-keyed row IS the same-user gate: another user's
id is simply "no row" → 404. fresh() auto-rotates within the refreshSkew
window; static providers degenerate to a plain kmsGet of Secrets[0]. Refresh
tokens are NEVER returned — custody keeps the sink. The token is never logged.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
ID is the connector id, provider + ":" + label ("openai:default") — the
auth-profile-id shape. Another user's id is simply no row, so 404.

post.summary: Is the direct intake path: a customer-held token/setup-token (Verify) or an externally obtained OAuth bundle from the CLI's local PKCE (Adopt).
post.description:
Is the direct intake path: a customer-held token/setup-token
(Verify) or an externally obtained OAuth bundle from the CLI's local PKCE
(Adopt). ALWAYS verify-before-store: a bad credential is refused and NOTHING
is persisted (connectByCredential's fail-closed order).

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: Provider is the user-scoped provider's registry id, from the path.

post.summary: Begins a device sign-in and returns the code to show the user plus how to poll for completion.
post.description:
Begins a device sign-in and returns the code to show the user plus
how to poll for completion. KMS readiness is checked NOW rather than dead-ending
the user at poll-done (connect() parity), and the per-provider connector cap is
checked before the provider is called. The provider's device code is persisted
only in the encrypted grants table and is NEVER returned.

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: Provider is the user-scoped provider's registry id, from the path.

post.summary: Advances a device sign-in.
post.description:
Advances a device sign-in. Terminal outcomes are DATA, not errors
(verifyConn {active:false} discipline) — the status set is closed:
pending|connected|denied|expired. pollSlow collapses to "pending" on the
wire; the raised cadence rides interval.

parameters.name: provider
parameters.description: Provider is the user-scoped provider's registry id, from the path.

parameters.name: flow
parameters.description:
Flow is the id deviceStartOut returned. Expired or another user's flow is
indistinguishable from an unknown one: 404.

get.summary: Returns every registered integration provider together with THIS org's connection status for it — the catalog the console's Integrations page renders.
get.description:
Returns every registered integration provider together with THIS org's
connection status for it — the catalog the console's Integrations page renders.
Org-authed: a caller with no validated principal is 403, because the status is
per-org and there is no org-less answer. User-plane providers (the /v1/connection
surface) are omitted; the two planes are disjoint.

post.summary: Discord interactions endpoint
post.description:
The Interactions Endpoint URL for the Discord app. It answers Discord's PING with a PONG, and handles the `/hanzo` slash command by acknowledging with a deferred ephemeral reply and editing that reply with the answer once the agent has run. Any other interaction is acknowledged and ignored.

Requests are verified by ED25519 SIGNATURE over the timestamp and body against the app's public key — not by HMAC, unlike the Slack webhooks. Interactions work over plain HTTP, so no gateway connection and no message-content intent is involved.

Discord does not retry, so this is the one channel where being at capacity is shown to the user as an ephemeral ask-to-run-it-again rather than answered as a retriable failure — nothing is recorded either way, so the next attempt is clean.

The caller here is the PLATFORM, not a Hanzo tenant, so there is no bearer and no principal. The signature check IS the authentication, and it fails closed. The tenant is never read from the payload either: it is resolved from the verified platform identifier through the connection map, so an event from a workspace nobody connected does nothing. Refusals are written with their own status rather than being flattened to a 500, so a rejected signature reads as 401 and a malformed body as 400.

get.summary: Begin linking a Hanzo account from Discord
get.description:
The entry point behind the connect prompt Hanzo shows in a Discord server. It starts a link session and redirects to Discord's OAuth `identify` consent — the narrowest scope that establishes which Discord user is asking, and nothing more.

This is one leg of a three-leg flow, and the legs are not interchangeable: a browser is expected to arrive here only from the leg before it. The link URL's state proves the prompt was server-minted and carries the CHAT it started from — it is provenance only, and it never decides which account gets linked. The account identity always comes from the platform's own verified sign-in and a host-bound cookie, so forwarding a link to someone else cannot bind their account, and a session lifted into another browser is refused rather than completed. Each link is single-use, and a deployment without linking configured answers 503.

get.summary: Complete the Discord account link
get.description:
The final leg: it binds the verified Discord user to the Hanzo account that just signed in, and answers a short confirmation page telling them to return to Discord. The Hanzo credential is sealed into the connected org's KMS namespace rather than stored beside the link.

This is one leg of a three-leg flow, and the legs are not interchangeable: a browser is expected to arrive here only from the leg before it. The link URL's state proves the prompt was server-minted and carries the CHAT it started from — it is provenance only, and it never decides which account gets linked. The account identity always comes from the platform's own verified sign-in and a host-bound cookie, so forwarding a link to someone else cannot bind their account, and a session lifted into another browser is refused rather than completed. Each link is single-use, and a deployment without linking configured answers 503.

get.summary: Discord sign-in return leg
get.description:
Where Discord returns the user after the identify consent. It resolves the verified Discord user, confirms the server is connected to an org, and hands the browser to the Hanzo sign-in that completes the link.

This is one leg of a three-leg flow, and the legs are not interchangeable: a browser is expected to arrive here only from the leg before it. The link URL's state proves the prompt was server-minted and carries the CHAT it started from — it is provenance only, and it never decides which account gets linked. The account identity always comes from the platform's own verified sign-in and a host-bound cookie, so forwarding a link to someone else cannot bind their account, and a session lifted into another browser is refused rather than completed. post.summary: Forge workflow_job webhook
post.description: Receives the forge's workflow_job delivery. The signature over the raw body is checked against the secret at KMS forge.WebhookRef before anything is decoded; a queued job becomes one ephemeral runner Job on the cluster, minted a registration token for exactly that job. A job of a pull request, of any action, also writes what its commit's runs say to GitHub as the commit status hanzo/ci. Every other action is answered 200 and ignored.

post.summary: Binds installations the App ALREADY holds to the org the caller is acting in — the reconciliation for a grant that happened outside our connect flow.
post.description:
Binds installations the App ALREADY holds to the org the caller is
acting in — the reconciliation for a grant that happened outside our connect
flow.

An installation IS the grant: GitHub recorded the consent when the App was
installed, and our connection row is bookkeeping that never got written because
nobody came through our callback. This writes that row from the App's own view,
so 23 accounts granted straight from GitHub stop reading as nothing.

The org is taken from the VALIDATED PRINCIPAL and never from the body, because
it is the one part GitHub cannot tell us. An installation carries an account
login, a type and a repository selection — nothing that names a Hanzo org. So
the binding cannot be DERIVED, only asserted, and the only unforgeable assertion
available is the org the caller is already acting in. Inferring one from the
account name would be a guess the store cannot catch: its key is
(org,provider,owner), so a wrong org is a valid row, and a valid row is a
mirror pointed at the wrong tenant.

SUPER ADMIN only, for that same reason. A tenant's proof that an account is
theirs is GitHub's own consent screen — the connect flow — and without it any
org could claim any account the App holds. Platform sudo is already the scope
that reads the whole install list, so it is the scope that may bind from it;
giving a tenant this verb would hand it every other tenant's repositories.

Idempotent: the row is keyed (org,provider,owner) and connected_at survives an
upsert, so claiming twice rebinds the same account to the same org and reports
it under `already`. Re-claiming also REFRESHES the installation id, so an
account reinstalled on GitHub — new id, same login — self-heals instead of
minting tokens against a dead installation.

Claiming an account another org holds ADDS this org's row and leaves theirs
standing, so no org loses an integration it is using.

post.summary: Forks a granted repository.
post.description:
Forks a granted repository.

GitHub's fork is ASYNCHRONOUS: it answers 202 with the target repo and
populates it in the background, and it answers the same 202 when the fork
already exists. So this reports what GitHub said rather than waiting — a call
that blocked until the clone finished would time out on a large repository and
tell the caller nothing it does not already know.

get.summary: Lists the GitHub accounts the caller may see the App installed on, each confirmed against the App's own list, plus where to add another.
get.description:
Lists the GitHub accounts the caller may see the App
installed on, each confirmed against the App's own list, plus where to add
another.

The confirmation is the point. A connection row holds an installation id, and
an id whose installation was since removed on GitHub is a row that mints
nothing — every list and import against it fails with a token error, which
reads as "our git integration is broken" rather than "that install is gone".
Checking the App's view turns that into a fact the caller can act on.

ORG-SCOPED for a tenant, deliberately. The App is installed across every
customer, so the raw list is the customer list; a tenant sees only accounts its
own org has bound. It discovers a NEW account by installing it (InstallURL),
which is GitHub's own consent screen — not by reading ours.

A SUPER ADMIN sees the App's whole install list, because that list is the
platform's own inventory rather than any one tenant's data, and platform sudo
is the single cross-tenant scope this house has. Without it an App installed
out-of-band — granted straight from GitHub, so no connect flow ever ran and no
connection row exists — is invisible to everyone: the console card reads "not
connected" and an operator asked "which GitHub orgs do you see" can only
answer for accounts already bound, which is precisely the accounts that were
never the question.

post.summary: Seeds the native todo with the EXISTING issues across the org's granted repos (default state=open); the webhook keeps them live thereafter.
post.description:
Seeds the native todo with the EXISTING issues across the
org's granted repos (default state=open); the webhook keeps them live thereafter.
Org-scoped by the validated principal — a caller only ever backfills its OWN org.
Synchronous + bounded (a total time budget and an issue cap) so it returns the
counts directly; idempotent by ExtRef, so a re-run continues where a truncated
pass left off and never duplicates.

get.summary: Lists the GitHub repositories the caller may work on, most recently pushed first, searched and paged on the server.
get.description:
Lists the GitHub repositories the caller may work on, most
recently pushed first, searched and paged on the server.

A person who connected their own GitHub sees what their token reaches in this
App's installations. An org admin who has not sees every repository in the
installations their org holds. Anyone else gets an empty page with
connected:false, which is the console's cue to ask them to connect.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Q keeps repositories whose owner/name contains it, case-insensitively.

parameters.description: Owner keeps one GitHub account's repositories — an org or a user login.

parameters.description: Limit is the page size: 1 to 100, and 50 when absent or unreadable.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description:
After is the `next` of the previous page. Absent starts at the most

post.summary: Imports the selected (or all) granted repos into git.hanzo.ai.
post.description:
Imports the selected (or all) granted repos into git.hanzo.ai. The
selection is intersected with the installation's GRANTED set, so a client can
never import a repo the App was not granted (org isolation + a grant check). The
import runs in a bounded background worker (don't block the request), so the
answer is 202 Accepted; poll GET /v1/git/repos for each repository to appear
on git.hanzo.ai.

get.description:
Lists a repository's branches, the default first, with prefix
search. The repository must be one the caller may see — the same set
GET /v1/provider/github/repos lists — or it is 404.

parameters.description: Owner is the GitHub account that holds the repository.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Repo is the repository's name within that account.

parameters.description: Q keeps branches whose name starts with it, matched by GitHub.

parameters.description: Limit is the page size: 1 to 100, and 50 when absent or unreadable.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: After is the `next` of the previous page.

Deletes the repo's Pages site. 404 when there is none, so a
caller can tell "turned it off" from "there was nothing on".

get.description:
Returns the repo's Pages status, live URL, custom domain and build

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description:
Repo is the repository's short name within the org's installation, with no

post.summary: Creates the repo's Pages site and answers 201 Created with it.
post.description:
Creates the repo's Pages site and answers 201 Created with it.
With buildType "workflow" the site builds via GitHub Actions; otherwise it builds
from a branch source, defaulting to the repo's own default branch when none is
given. Only "/" and "/docs" are legal source paths (GitHub's rule).

parameters.name: repo

put.description:
Sets or clears the custom domain (cname) and updates HTTPS

parameters.description: Repo is the repository, from the :repo path segment.

post.description:
Requests a Pages rebuild and returns the queued build's status.
The build is queued AT GITHUB, not completed here, so the answer is 202 Accepted
and its status is the one GitHub reported at queue time. 404 when the repository
has no Pages site, or when the org's installation was not granted it.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description:
Repo is the repository's short name within the org's installation, with no
owner prefix (the owner is server-derived from the grant). A trailing ".git"
is stripped.

post.summary: Finds repositories on GitHub.
post.description:
Finds repositories on GitHub.

This reads the PUBLIC index and returns nothing an installation unlocks: it is
how you find a repository to fork, not a way to see inside one. The org's own
token is used only so the query is rate-limited against the installation
rather than anonymously — the results are the same ones anyone would get.

burns its nonce, and parks the code for the return page to complete; it

post.description:
Finishes connecting the caller's GitHub account: it takes
the authorization the callback parked, trades it for the person's token, and

person's grant id is simply not found — and a grant completes once.

post.description:
Begins connecting the caller's own GitHub account: it answers
the App's authorization page, carrying a state signed for this org and this
person. Every member may connect their own; it grants nothing the person does
not already hold on GitHub. The page shows GitHub's account picker (githubPick),
so a connect after a Disconnect can choose another account: GitHub otherwise
skips the page for anyone who authorized the App before.

post.description:
Forgets the caller's GitHub connection in this org: the
token is revoked at GitHub, and the sealed secrets and the row go. It says
whether GitHub confirmed the revocation rather than reporting a success it did
not see. Disconnecting what is not connected succeeds.

post.summary: GitHub App webhook
post.description:
The address the GitHub App delivers events to. A push is handed to the repository sync engine, and an issue or issue-comment event is mirrored into the native todo — idempotently, so the same issue re-syncs to one row however many times it is edited, closed or reopened. A repository event that puts a repo INTO the granted set (created, transferred, unarchived) raises one todo offering to import it; accepting means POSTing that repo to /v1/provider/github/import. It never imports on its own.

It answers a benign 200 for everything it does not act on — the ping, other event types, an unknown installation — deliberately, so GitHub does not enter a retry storm over events that were never going to do anything. Only a bad signature and a genuine sync failure are non-200, and an oversized payload is refused outright.

Two sync rules are worth stating because neither is guessable. EVERY ref syncs, tags as well as branches, because releases are cut by tag and filtering them would stop publishing with nothing reporting a failure. And a delete is NEVER propagated: the native side is canonical, so an inbound delete never removes a native ref.

The payload is verified by HMAC against the webhook secret before it is parsed.

The caller here is the PLATFORM, not a Hanzo tenant, so there is no bearer and no principal. The signature check IS the authentication, and it fails closed. The tenant is never read from the payload either: it is resolved from the verified platform identifier through the connection map, so an event from a workspace nobody connected does nothing. Refusals are written with their own status rather than being flattened to a 500, so a rejected signature reads as 401 and a malformed body as 400.

post.summary: Binds the caller's Linear organization to the org and seals the webhook secret.
post.description:
Binds the caller's Linear organization to the org and seals the
webhook secret. The organization is READ from the caller's own key, never taken

post.description:
Posts a comment on a Linear issue with the caller's own key, so it
carries their name. This is the op an agent is offered when it should answer in

post.description:
Seeds the native todo with the EXISTING Linear issues the
caller's key can see (default state=open); the webhook keeps them live
thereafter. Synchronous and bounded, idempotent by ExtRef.

post.summary: Linear webhook
post.description:
The address Linear delivers Issue and Comment events to. An issue event is mirrored into the native todo — idempotently by identifier, so ENG-123 is one row however many times it is edited, moved or closed — and every issue and comment event is handed to the automations engine as a verified trigger, which is how an org runs an agent when an issue is assigned to it or a comment mentions it. A remove is never propagated: the native side is canonical.

It answers a benign 200 for what it does not act on — an unknown organization, other event types — so Linear does not retry-storm. A bad signature and a delivery older than a minute are 401; only a sink failure is 502.

The delivery names its Linear organization; that organization's own webhook secret — sealed at /v1/provider/linear/claim — verifies the HMAC over the raw body, so the tenant is the organization the signature proves, never a header.

The caller here is the PLATFORM, not a Hanzo tenant, so there is no bearer and no principal. The signature check IS the authentication, and it fails closed. The tenant is never read from the payload either: it is resolved from the verified platform identifier through the connection map, so an event from a workspace nobody connected does nothing. Refusals are written with their own status rather than being flattened to a 500, so a rejected signature reads as 401 and a malformed body as 400.

post.summary: Receive OpenRouter Broadcast traces as usage rows
post.description:
OpenRouter's spend is invisible to every Hanzo money lens because those lenses read hanzo.cloud_usage and OpenRouter meters keys of its own. Point a Broadcast destination (Settings ▸ Observability ▸ Webhook) at this endpoint and each generation span becomes ONE row in that same ledger with provider `openrouter`, so one query answers what we spend everywhere. Enable the Cost and Identity field categories: cost is the money and identity carries `openrouter.api_key_name`, which is what says WHICH key spent it — it lands in `account` as openrouter/<key name>.

AUTHENTICATION IS A HANZO KEY. Broadcast signs nothing; its only authentication is the destination's Headers map, so send a key as `Authorization: Bearer pk-…` and it is admitted exactly as /v1/event admits a beacon's: a project key resolves through the project that minted it, an IAM-issued key through IAM. That key names the org every row is filed under; it can write and cannot read. No key, or a key that names no org, is 401 and nothing is stored.

The body is OTLP/JSON — `{resourceSpans:[{scopeSpans:[{spans:[…]}]}]}` — exactly as OpenTelemetry defines it; the model, tokens and cost are read from each span's `gen_ai.*` attributes and the key name from `openrouter.api_key_name`. The answer is `{stored, dropped}`: how many generations became rows, and how many spans named no model. Those are OpenRouter's trace and span parents — they carry no cost to meter. An empty payload stores nothing and answers 200, which is what makes Test Connection pass. A warehouse that cannot take the rows answers 503 so the delivery shows red and can be replayed: a row is keyed by its span id, so a redelivery collapses rather than double-counting.

get.summary: Lists Slack conversations for the caller's connected workspace.
get.description:
Lists Slack conversations for the caller's connected workspace.
Read next_cursor until empty to discover channels, including private channels
or group DMs when types requests them and the bot has their read scopes.

parameters.name: types
parameters.description:
Types selects public_channel, private_channel, im or mpim, comma-separated.
Defaults to public_channel; each selected type requires its own read scope.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Cursor continues the previous page's next_cursor.

post.summary: Slack slash command webhook
post.description:
The address Slack posts a slash command to, form-encoded. It acknowledges inside Slack's three-second budget and posts the answer afterwards to the command's own response URL, which is why the immediate reply is empty.

The body is verified against the same app signing secret as the events webhook, and a repeat of the same command invocation is absorbed rather than answered twice.

The caller here is the PLATFORM, not a Hanzo tenant, so there is no bearer and no principal. The signature check IS the authentication, and it fails closed. The tenant is never read from the payload either: it is resolved from the verified platform identifier through the connection map, so an event from a workspace nobody connected does nothing. Refusals are written with their own status rather than being flattened to a 500, so a rejected signature reads as 401 and a malformed body as 400.

The answer is acknowledged immediately and the work happens afterwards, because every one of these platforms times out a slow webhook. Duplicate deliveries are absorbed durably, so a platform retry of an event that already ran never runs it a second time or bills for it twice. When the agent pool is full nothing at all is recorded and the delivery is refused as retriable, so the message is re-delivered later rather than being lost or half-processed.

post.summary: Slack Events API webhook
post.description:
The address a Slack app posts workspace events to. It answers Slack's url_verification handshake with the challenge, and routes an @mention or a direct message to an agent turn that replies in the same thread. The turn holds the product's own tools, so a request to change code starts a sandbox run because the model chose to — there is no prefix and no second path.

The raw body and its timestamp are verified against the app's signing secret before anything is read from them. Hanzo's own bot messages are dropped, so a reply cannot trigger another reply.

Refusals are written with their own status rather than being flattened to a 500, so a rejected signature reads as 401 and a malformed body as 400.

get.summary: OAuth return for any connector
get.description:
The single address every connector's OAuth flow returns to. It exchanges the authorization the provider granted, records the connection, and ALWAYS redirects the browser back to the console — on success and on every labeled failure alike, so a user never lands on a raw JSON dead end.

It is public and carries no principal, so the org is taken ONLY from the signed state minted when the flow began; no header is trusted here. That state is single-use and is burned BEFORE the exchange, so one authorization is one attempt and a replayed return fails instead of exchanging twice.

Tokens are sealed into the org's KMS namespace BEFORE the connection row is written, so a failure of the secret store leaves no half-connected integration advertising a credential that was never stored. Token values never appear in the redirect, in a log line or in an error.

One generalization is worth knowing: a GitHub App installation returns an installation identifier instead of an OAuth code, and it is accepted in the code's place so the App model needs no second address.

A GitHub connect that returns from GitHub's authorization page, rather than its install page, answers a short page instead of a redirect when the person already controls installations no organization holds: they choose which one to connect, or go on to install the app on another account. Nothing is bound until they choose.

post.description:

It binds the chosen account to the organization that started the connect and redirects back to the page that asked, as the callback does.

It is public and carries no principal. Its authority is the token alone: signed like the callback's state, carrying the offered accounts under its signature, and single-use, so a page answers once and only with an account it offered.

single-use nonce plus an HMAC-signed state that binds this org to this provider,
and answering with the provider's authorize URL for the caller to redirect to.

Fail-closed order, unchanged: no principal → 403; unknown provider → 404; an
AdminOnly connector without the caller's own-org admin bit → 403; not configured
→ 503; KMS not ready → 503 (the flow WILL need to seal a token, so refuse now
rather than dead-end at the callback).

account.description:
Account names ONE account to disconnect — the label the connection carries
(a GitHub login, for the App) or its platform id (a Page, a channel, a
board). Empty disconnects every account the org holds for the provider. An
account the org does not hold disconnects nothing.

provider.description: Provider is the connector's registry id, from the :provider path segment.

accounts.description:
Accounts are the account labels this disconnect removed. Omitted when none
was connected.

disconnected.description: Disconnected is always true — the org's secrets and connection row are gone.

uninstalled.description:
Uninstalled are the accounts whose provider installation was removed too,
because no other org held them. An account another org still holds keeps its
installation and is absent here.

repo.description:
Repo narrows the pass to ONE granted repository, named `owner/name` or
bare `name` (case-insensitive). Empty walks every granted repository. A
project page syncs its own issues with this; the org-wide pass stays the
default. A name the connection does not grant is a 404, never a silent
empty pass that reads as "this repository has no issues".

state.description:
State is the GitHub issue state to walk: "open" (the default), "closed" or
"all". Anything else is a 400.

created.description: Created is how many native issues this pass created.

failed.description: Failed is how many repos or issues errored; the pass continues past each.

issues.description: Issues is how many upstream issues were seen.

repos.description: Repos is how many granted repos were walked (archived/disabled are skipped).

truncated.description:
Truncated is set when the time budget or the issue cap stopped the pass early.
Re-run to continue — the mirror is idempotent by ExtRef, so nothing duplicates.

updated.description: Updated is how many existing native issues this pass refreshed.

commit.description: Commit is the sha the branch points at.

default.description:
Default is whether it is the repository's default branch, which always
leads the first page when it matches.

name.description: Name is the branch's short name ("main", "feat/login").

branches.description:
Branches is this page: the default branch first, then the rest by name.
Never null.

next.description: Next is the cursor for the page after this one; empty on the last page.

total.description: Total is how many branches match q, across every page.

accounts.description:
Accounts names GitHub logins the App is installed on ("hanzoai"). Matched
case-insensitively, since GitHub logins are. Ignored when all is true.

all.description: All binds every account the App holds, instead of naming them.

already.description: Already were bound before the call and are unchanged by it.

claimed.description: Claimed are the accounts this call bound. Never null; [] when none.

clone_url.description:
CloneURL is the fork's https git remote. GitHub populates a new fork in the
background, so a clone issued the moment this answers can still find it empty.

default_branch.description: DefaultBranch is the branch the fork checks out, inherited from upstream.

existing.description:
Existing reports that the fork was already there. GitHub answers 202 either
way, so without this a caller cannot tell "made you one" from "you had one".

full_name.description:
FullName is the fork's "owner/repo". The owner is the account it landed in
— the request's org, or the installation's own account when none was named.

html_url.description: HTMLURL is the fork's page on github.com.

org.description:
Org is the GitHub account to fork INTO; empty forks to the installation's
own account, which is the common case.

repo.description: Repo is a repository the org's installation was GRANTED, by name.

all.description:
All imports every repository the installation grants, instead of naming
them. Archived and disabled repositories are skipped either way — they
cannot be fetched.

repos.description:
Repos names the repositories to import, either owner-qualified
("hanzo-apps/ai") or as a bare name ("ai"); a trailing ".git" is stripped.
A bare name that matches more than one granted repository is an error
rather than a guess, because one Hanzo org may hold several GitHub
installations and a name is only unique within an owner.
Ignored when all is true.

codebases.description:
Codebases are the names they take in the org's code workspace, in the same
order: poll GET /v1/git/repos for each to appear.

queued.description: Queued is how many repositories were handed to the background importer.

repos.description: Repos names those repositories, in the installation's listing order.

connected.description: Connected reports whether THIS org has already bound this account.

grant.description:
Grant is "all" or "selected" — how many of the account's repositories the
install covers. A reader deciding what to import needs the reach, not just
the name.

htmlUrl.description: HTMLURL is the account's page on GitHub.

login.description: Login is the GitHub account name — the org or user the App is installed on.

installUrl.description:
InstallURL is where to grant a new account, so a UI with an empty list has
somewhere to send the reader instead of a dead end.

installations.description:
Installations is every account the caller may see: the ones its own org has
bound, or — for a super admin — every account the App is installed on.
Never null; [] when none.

repo.description: Repo is the repository the build was queued for.

status.description: Status is GitHub's build state at the moment it was queued ("queued").

url.description: URL is GitHub's API URL for the build, for polling it there.

disabled.description: Disabled is always true — a failure is an HTTP error, never this shape.

repo.description: Repo is the repository whose site was deleted.

branch.description:
Branch is the legacy source branch; empty defaults to the repo's own default
branch. Ignored when buildType is "workflow".

buildType.description:
BuildType selects the builder: "workflow" builds via GitHub Actions, anything
else builds from the branch source above.

path.description:
Path is the source directory within the branch: "/" (the default) or "/docs".
GitHub allows no others.

repo.description: Repo is the repository, from the :repo path segment.

branch.description: Branch is the branch the site builds from.

path.description: Path is the directory within that branch: "/" or "/docs".

branch.description: Branch switches the legacy source branch. Empty leaves the source alone.

buildType.description: BuildType switches the builder: "legacy" or "workflow". Empty leaves it.

cname.description:
CNAME is the custom domain. Omit to leave it alone, "" to clear it, or a
valid FQDN to set it.

httpsEnforced.description: HTTPSEnforced toggles GitHub's enforce-HTTPS bit. Omit to leave it alone.

path.description:
Path is the source directory to pair with Branch: "/" (the default) or
"/docs". Read only when Branch is given.

repo.description: Repo is the repository, from the :repo path segment.
Repo is the repository that was updated.

updated.description: Updated is always true — a failure is an HTTP error, never this shape.

buildType.description: BuildType is the builder in use: "legacy" (branch source) or "workflow".

cname.description: CNAME is the custom domain, absent when none is set.

custom404.description: Custom404 is whether the repo ships its own 404 page.

repo.description: Repo is the repository the site belongs to.

source.description: Source is the branch + path the site builds from. Absent under "workflow".

status.description:
Status is GitHub's build state: "built", "building" or "errored". Absent
before the first build.

url.description: URL is the live site (GitHub's html_url).

codebase.description:
Codebase is the name it has in the org's code workspace once brought in
(POST /v1/provider/github/repos/import): listed by GET /v1/git/repos when
it is there.

default_branch.description: DefaultBranch is the branch GitHub opens it on.

full_name.description:
FullName is owner/name, the address a coding run, a branch listing and a
deploy take.

installation_id.description:
InstallationID is the installation of the Hanzo Platform App that reaches
it — the grant a run on it is minted from.

name.description: Name is its name within that account.

owner.description: Owner is the GitHub account that holds it.

pushed_at.description:
PushedAt is when anything was last pushed to it, RFC 3339 UTC. Absent for a
repository nothing was ever pushed to.

connected.description:
Connected is whether this answer is the caller's OWN GitHub. False with
repositories is an org admin seeing the org's installations; false with none
is the cue to connect.

next.description: Next is the cursor for the page after this one; empty on the last page.

repos.description: Repos is this page, most recently pushed first. Never null.

total.description: Total is how many repositories match q and owner, across every page.

unread.description:
Unread names the installations that could not be read, so a short list is
distinguishable from a complete one. Absent when the answer is whole.

clone_url.description: CloneURL is the repository's https git remote.

default_branch.description: DefaultBranch is the branch a clone checks out.

description.description: Description is the blurb the repository's owner wrote. Empty when it has none.

full_name.description:
FullName is the repository's "owner/repo" on GitHub. Finding it here does
NOT make it forkable: githubFork takes a repo the org's installation was
granted, and a hit from the public index usually is not one.

html_url.description: HTMLURL is the repository's page on github.com.

language.description:
Language is the primary language GitHub detected from the file mix ("Go",
"TypeScript"). Empty when GitHub attributes none.

private.description:
Private is GitHub's visibility flag, passed through. This op reads the
public index — the org's token only charges the rate limit to the
installation — so it is false for everything a search can reach.

stars.description:
Stars is GitHub's stargazers_count as the SEARCH INDEX held it when the
query ran — a snapshot, not a live count off the repository.

count.description:
Count is how many hits Repos carries. It is that array's length, NOT
GitHub's total_count, so it never exceeds limit and says nothing about how
many more repositories matched.

repos.description:
Repos are the matching repositories in GitHub's own relevance order, capped
at limit. Always an array, never null.

limit.description:
Limit caps the answer; 0 takes the default and anything above the ceiling
is clamped rather than refused.

q.description:
Q is GitHub's own search syntax, passed through: "tetris language:go",
"org:hanzoai stars:>10". Passing it through rather than inventing a
vocabulary means one thing to learn, and it is theirs.

grant.description:
Grant is the id the callback handed the console in its redirect. It is
single-use, lives ten minutes, and is readable only by the person who
started the flow.

return.description:
Return is the page the callback sends the person back to, with
complete=github&grant=<id> (or error=github&reason=<why>) added to its
query. It must name one of this deployment's return pages (on
api.hanzo.ai: https://hanzo.ai/?at=-/settings/integrations,
https://console.hanzo.ai/connectors, https://platform.hanzo.ai/connectors);
anything else, or nothing, returns to the console's /connectors.

authorizeUrl.description:
AuthorizeURL is GitHub's authorization page for the App. GitHub returns the
browser to the callback, which parks the answer and sends it on with
complete=github&grant=<id> — to the return page the connect named, or the
console's /connectors — and that page POSTs the grant to
/v1/provider/github/user/complete.

disconnected.description:
Disconnected is always true: the sealed token and the connection are gone
from this deployment. A custody failure is an HTTP error instead.

revoked.description:
Revoked is whether GitHub confirmed the token is dead. False means GitHub
could not be told — the token lives until it expires or is revoked from
the person's GitHub settings — or there was no token to revoke.

configured.description:
Configured is whether this deployment holds the App's OAuth client. False
means nobody can connect here yet, and connect answers 503.

connected.description:
Connected is whether the caller has connected their own GitHub account in
this org. False means their repositories come from nowhere: an org admin
still sees the org's installations, and everyone else is asked to connect.

connectedAt.description: ConnectedAt is when the connection was made, RFC 3339 UTC.

expiresAt.description:
ExpiresAt is when the current access token expires, RFC 3339 UTC. It is
rotated before it does; absent for a token GitHub does not expire.

login.description: Login is the GitHub account they connected. Absent when not connected.

cloneUrl.description: CloneURL is the https remote to clone.

defaultBranch.description:
DefaultBranch is the branch a clone lands on ("main" when GitLab names none,
which is what an empty project reports).

description.description: Description is the project's own, empty when it has none.

fullName.description:
FullName is the namespace path ("acme/widgets", "acme/team/widgets" for a
subgroup) — the string GitLab calls path_with_namespace.

name.description: Name is the project's path segment ("widgets"), not its display name.

private.description: Private is true for anything not publicly visible (private or internal).

pushedAt.description: PushedAt is RFC3339 last activity, so a client can sort or say "2h ago".

account.description:
Account is the connected GitLab username, so a client can label the list
without a second call. Empty when the connection recorded none.

projects.description:
Projects is every project the token reaches, newest activity first. Never
null; [] when the account has none.

grant.description:
Grant is the id the callback handed the page in its redirect. It is
single-use, lives ten minutes, and is readable only by the person who
started the flow.

return.description:
Return is the page the callback sends the person back to, with
complete=google&grant=<id> (or error=google&reason=<why>) added to its
query. It must name one of this deployment's return pages; anything else,
or nothing, returns to the console's /connectors.

authorizeUrl.description:
AuthorizeURL is Google's consent page. Google returns the browser to the
callback, which parks the answer and sends it on with
complete=google&grant=<id> — to the return page the connect named, or the
console's /connectors — and that page POSTs the grant to
/v1/provider/google/user/complete.

disconnected.description:
Disconnected is always true: the sealed tokens and the connection are gone
from this deployment. A custody failure is an HTTP error instead.

revoked.description:
Revoked is whether Google confirmed the grant is dead. False means Google
could not be told — the grant lives until the person removes it from their
Google account — or there was nothing to revoke.

configured.description:
Configured is whether this deployment holds the OAuth client. False means
nobody can connect here yet, and connect answers 503.

connected.description:
Connected is whether the caller has connected their own Google account in
this org.

connectedAt.description: ConnectedAt is when the connection was made, RFC 3339 UTC.

email.description:
Email is the Google account they connected: the From of every message sent
as them. Absent when not connected.

expiresAt.description:
ExpiresAt is when the current access token expires, RFC 3339 UTC. It is
rotated before it does.

send.description:
Send is whether the grant lets Hanzo send mail as them. A connection is only
kept when it does, so this is Connected unless the person later narrowed
the grant at Google.

channel.description: Channel is Slack's id for the room that refused.

error.description: Error is Slack's own code, carried through unchanged.

name.description: Name is that room's human name, so the operator does not have to look the id up.

state.description: State is the set of issues to walk: "open" (the default), "closed" or "all".

created.description: Created is how many native issues this pass created.

failed.description: Failed is how many issues errored; the pass continues past each.

issues.description: Issues is how many Linear issues were seen.

truncated.description:
Truncated is set when the time budget or the issue cap stopped the pass early.
Re-run to continue — the mirror is idempotent by ExtRef, so nothing duplicates.

updated.description: Updated is how many existing native issues this pass refreshed.

secret.description:
Secret is the signing secret configured on the webhook in Linear. Claiming
again with a new value rotates it.

name.description: Name is the organization's URL key.

organization.description: Organization is the Linear organization id now bound to this org.

path.description: Path is the address to configure in Linear, on this deployment's origin.

issue.description: Issue is the issue's identifier (ENG-123) or its id.

id.description: ID is the comment's id in Linear.

url.description: URL is the comment's address in Linear.

providers.description: Providers is the whole catalog. Never null; [] when nothing is registered.

account.description: Account is the account label the flow reported; sanitized on ingest.

refresh.description: Refresh is the refresh token. It is sealed and NEVER handed back out.

description.description: Description says what it does. Only on GET /v1/provider/{provider}.

displayName.description: DisplayName is what the card calls it.

name.description: Name is the action's id — what a run or a flow step names.

props.description:
Props are its inputs — what POST /v1/provider/{provider}/run takes as
input. Only on GET /v1/provider/{provider}; the list names actions only.

accounts.description:
Accounts is every account this org has connected for the provider, each
with its own platform id. Tokens never appear here.

actions.description:
Actions are what the connector can be asked to do, by a flow step or an
agent (POST /v1/provider/{provider}/run when Runnable).

app.description:
App names the OAuth app registration its sign-in uses ("GOOGLE"), for a
connector whose sign-in awaits one.

available.description:
Available is whether THIS DEPLOYMENT has the provider's app credentials, so
connect can succeed. False renders the card without a working Connect button.

checks.description:
Checks is whether a pasted credential is checked with the provider before
it is stored. False means it is sealed on its shape and checked on use.

connected.description: Connected is whether this org has a live connection to the provider.

connection.description:
Connection is the connected account's non-secret detail. Absent when the org
has no connection; tokens NEVER appear here (they live only in KMS).
When the org holds several accounts, this is the first and Accounts is
every one of them.

description.description: Description is the one-line pitch the console card shows.

fields.description: Fields is the form a credential connector asks for. Absent otherwise.

id.description: ID is the provider's registry id and the :provider path segment ("slack").

kind.description:
Kind is how a reader connects it NOW: "oauth" (send the browser to the
provider), "credential" (fill in Fields), "device" (enter a code), or
"none" (nothing to connect — ready, or not connectable here; Note says).

logo.description: Logo is where the connector's logo is served. Absent when it has none.

modes.description:
Modes are the ways this provider can be connected, derived from what it
actually declares — "managed", "oauth", "apikey", "device", "mcp". One
console page renders every card from this field rather than carrying a
table of its own, which is how a provider added here shows up there
without a second edit.

name.description: Name is the provider's display name ("Slack").

note.description: Note says why the connector cannot be connected here, when it cannot.

runnable.description: Runnable is whether its actions run on this deployment.

scopes.description: Scopes are the permissions a connection will ask for. Never null.

triggers.description: Triggers are the events a flow can start on.

connector.description: Connection is the connector with its new expiry.

refreshed.description: Refreshed is always true — a failed rotation is an HTTP error.

action.description: Action is the action's name, as GET /v1/provider/{provider} lists it.

input.description: Input is the action's props, by name.

provider.description: Provider is the connector, from the path.

error.description: Error is why the action failed, when it did.

ok.description: Ok is whether the action ran to completion.

output.description: Output is the action's result when it ran; its shape is the action's own.

channels.description: Channels contains one page of conversations visible to the bot.

next_cursor.description: NextCursor is empty when there are no more pages.

id.description: ID is the channel ID to pass to message reads and sends.

is_member.description: IsMember reports whether Hanzo has joined this channel.

is_mpim.description: IsMPIM identifies a group direct message.

is_private.description: IsPrivate identifies a private channel or conversation.

name.description: Name is the channel name, without #. DMs may have no name.

channel.description: Channel is the resolved channel ID the message was in.

ts.description: TS is the deleted message's timestamp, which now addresses nothing.

id.description: ID is the file's Slack ID and the handle the file read takes.

mimetype.description:
Mimetype is the type Slack recorded at upload. It is the uploader's word,
so it describes the file rather than deciding how the bytes are served.

name.description: Name is the filename as uploaded.

permalink.description:
Permalink opens the file in Slack, for a person. It needs a Slack session
and is never the bytes.

size.description: Size is the file's length in bytes.

title.description: Title is the title Slack displays, which may differ from the filename.

already.description:
Already counts the channels it was a member of before, kept apart from
Joined because only one of the two is a change.

failed.description: Failed is per-channel, so one refusal does not hide the rest of the walk.

joined.description: Joined names the channels this run walked into — the change it made.

listed.description: Listed is every public, unarchived channel the workspace has.

bot_id.description: BotID identifies a bot author when present.

files.description:
Files are the files attached to this message. Read one's bytes with
GET /v1/provider/slack/file?id=<id>; nothing here is the content.

reply_count.description: ReplyCount indicates whether a parent has replies to fetch separately.

subtype.description: Subtype distinguishes messages from channel events.

text.description: Text is the message in Slack's formatting.

thread_ts.description: ThreadTS is the parent timestamp for a threaded message.

ts.description: TS is Slack's exact message timestamp and ID; retain it as a string.

user.description: User is the author's Slack user ID.

channel.description: Channel is the resolved channel ID, reusable for further reads and replies.

has_more.description: HasMore indicates that Slack has additional messages beyond this page.

messages.description: Messages is one page, newest first for history and oldest first for threads.

next_cursor.description: NextCursor continues this query; never assume one page is the whole history.

channel.description: Channel is a Slack channel ID, name (#hanzo-gtm), or channel mention.

name.description: Name is the emoji's name WITHOUT colons — "eyes", not ":eyes:".

ts.description: TS is the exact timestamp of the message to react to.

channel.description: Channel is the resolved channel ID the message sits in.

name.description: Name is the emoji that was added, without colons.

ts.description: TS is the reacted-to message's exact Slack timestamp.

channel.description: Channel is the conversation ID the match sits in.

channel_name.description: ChannelName is that conversation's name, when Slack reports one.

permalink.description: Permalink addresses the message in a browser.

text.description: Text is the matching message's text.

ts.description:
TS is the message's exact Slack timestamp, the handle for replying to or
reacting to it.

user.description: User is the author's Slack user ID.

username.description: Username is the author's display name, when Slack reports one.

count.description: Count bounds the page, 1-100. Zero means 20.

page.description: Page is the 1-based page of results. Zero means the first.

query.description:
Query is Slack's own search syntax — bare words, or in:#channel,
from:@someone, before:2026-09-01, has:link.

matches.description: Matches are this page's hits, most relevant first.

page.description: Page is the page these matches came from.

pages.description: Pages is how many pages the query has in total.

total.description: Total is how many messages matched, across every page.

channel.description: Channel is a Slack channel ID, name (#hanzo-gtm), or Slack channel mention.

text.description: Text is the message to post as Hanzo, up to 40000 characters.

thread_ts.description: ThreadTS optionally replies under this parent message's exact ts.

channel.description: Channel is the resolved channel ID where the message was posted.

ts.description: TS is the posted message's exact Slack timestamp.

channel.description: Channel is a Slack channel ID, name (#hanzo-gtm), or channel mention.

text.description: Text is the replacement, up to 40000 characters.

ts.description: TS is the exact timestamp of the message to rewrite.

channel.description: Channel is the resolved channel ID the message sits in.

ts.description: TS is the rewritten message's exact Slack timestamp, unchanged by an edit.

expiresAt.description: ExpiresAt is when this token expires, RFC 3339 UTC; empty if non-expiring.

provider.description: Provider is the connector's provider id.

token.description: Token is the access token, rotated first if it was within the refresh window.

providers.description: Providers is every USER-scoped provider, sorted by id. Never null.

account.description: Account is the account label the provider reported. Present only when active.

active.description: Active is whether the stored credential verified live against the provider.

externalId.description: ExternalID is the provider's account id. Present only when active.

provider.description: Provider is the connector's registry id.

reason.description: Reason is why the check failed. Present only when active is false.

scopes.description: Scopes are the permissions the credential carries. Present only when active.

description.description: Description is the group's description. Optional, at most 2048 characters.

subject.description: Subject is the group's name, shown to its members. Required, at most 128 characters.

id.description: ID is the group id. A reply addresses it with recipient_type group.

invite_link.description:
InviteLink is the link a person opens to join. Anyone holding it can join,
so it is answered only to an org admin.

bearer.description: The caller's credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is either an access token minted by Hanzo IAM or an API key (pk-/sk-). X-Authorization, and HTTP Basic carrying the token as the password, are accepted spellings of the same header for clients that cannot set Authorization; a browser presents the session cookie instead. Every operation requires it unless it says `security: []`.
